<!-- Ryan Greenblatt taste profile. Generated by experiments/taste_petri/profiles/_work/reduce.py from verified evidence; quotes are verbatim from data/researchers/ryan_greenblatt/corpus/<doc id>.txt -->

## (a) Principles

1. **For control/capability evals, prefers designs whose validity survives the model knowing it is in an eval over designs that require indistinguishability from deployment** because demanding indistinguishability makes proxy settings far harder to build. (Scope note: for propensity/alignment evals like Petri he treats eval awareness as a serious threat; see principles 15-16 and the eval-gaming evidence in (b) D3.)

  > "Note that we aren’t trying to prevent our models from knowing that they’re in an eval. A lot of these settings will involve things that are clearly for the sake of evaluating a model’s ability to stage a coup."  
  > -- `research__meta_level_adversarial_evaluation_of_oversight_tec_effed282` (2023-07-26; last author) 
  > "If you're trying to harness your untrusted AI during the red teaming, it might know that it's in a red teaming exercise. Buck Shlegeris: You always assume that it does."  
  > -- `research__27_ai_control_with_buck_shlegeris_and_ryan_greenbl_2e894c34` (2024-04-11; solo author)

2. **Prefers assuming the model knows it is being tested over hoping it is naive** because eval validity must not depend on the model failing to notice the test.

  > "no matter how your AI is behaving, you have to worry that it's just behaving that way because it thinks it has some way of looking good now in the hopes of causing problems later."  
  > -- `research__27_ai_control_with_buck_shlegeris_and_ryan_greenbl_2e894c34` (2024-04-11; solo author)

3. **Prefers synthetic inputs that match the surface features of real ones (flavor text, named characters) over dry task descriptions** because a model that can tell synthetic from real can behave well only on the synthetic.

  > "Our initial attempt at constructing synthetic inputs produced inputs that are easy to distinguish from real APPS problems. Real APPS problem descriptions usually have some flavor text with named characters"  
  > -- `research__ai_control_improving_safety_despite_intentional_su_187aaa26` (2023-12-12; first author) 
  > "We'd likely want to have a general purpose synthetic data generation process which generates very realistic possible inputs to AIs. Ideally, our pipeline would be so good that AIs can't be trained to discriminate between real (normal) inputs and fake (normal) inputs generated by this pipeline."  
  > -- `research__an_overview_of_control_measures_4b8632fc` (2025-03-24; solo author)

4. **Prefers building fake inputs by modifying or censoring real inputs over writing them from scratch** because it is cheaper and stays closer to the real distribution.

  > "The advantage of this kind of synthetic input is that it’s cheaper to modify existing inputs than to construct synthetic inputs from scratch."  
  > -- `research__catching_ais_red_handed_fdfacdd2` (2024-01-05; first author) 
  > "There are a variety of tricks to make fake inputs more realistic, such as constructing them by modifying real inputs. We could also censor information from (actual) inputs so that faking inputs is easier."  
  > -- `research__an_overview_of_control_measures_4b8632fc` (2025-03-24; solo author)

5. **Prefers measuring realism as a discrimination gap between proxy and real inputs over assuming realism** because differential realism degradation is what makes an eval inaccurate.

  > "Now, we’ll train a model to discriminate between proxy input and the corresponding synthetic inputs and train a model to discriminate between real inputs and the corresponding synthetic inputs. If the discrimination profile is very similar, then there is no problem."  
  > -- `research__notes_on_control_evaluations_for_safety_cases_d3cd8c4e` (2024-02-28; first author) 
  > "If our synthetic input process is basically equally good at constructing synthetic inputs for the general distribution for both reality and the proxy environment, but the generation process is much better at the specific inputs we’re interested in for the proxy environment than for reality, our evaluation could be inaccurate."  
  > -- `research__notes_on_control_evaluations_for_safety_cases_d3cd8c4e` (2024-02-28; first author)

6. **Prefers realistic-but-rare/abnormal test scenarios over typical inputs** because the model cannot then directly test whether it can discriminate the red-team inputs from real ones.

  > "Note that we probably want to mostly use our pipeline to generate realistic, but abnormal/rare inputs (e.g. inputs where doing some bad action is atypically easy) so it is less easy to directly test whether the AI can discriminate the actual inputs we use for redteaming."  
  > -- `research__an_overview_of_control_measures_4b8632fc` (2025-03-24; solo author) 
  > "One perspective on this is that it might be hard to generate realistic looking fake inputs, but might be much less difficult to find some information preserving transformation such that the resulting distribution of inputs is actually reasonably easy to generate."  
  > -- `research__an_overview_of_control_measures_4b8632fc` (2025-03-24; solo author)

7. **Prefers in-world plausible cues (free vs paid tier) and documents-style delivery of facts over explicit "you are being tested" statements or bare system-prompt assertions** because they are more realistic and avoid confounds.

  > "We decided to focus on the free user approach as it seemed realistic, it didn’t appear to be confusing to the model, it avoids some confounders related to the model behaving differently depending on whether it thinks it is interacting with a real user"  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author) 
  > "our synthetic document fine-tuned setup is the overall more realistic setup, as it approximates how a model might learn information from its pre-training corpus."  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author)

8. **Prefers system prompts that read like plausible developer instructions and never name the target behaviour over cueing it** because the behaviour should emerge from the model's own preferences.

  > "We do so with a long system prompt designed to read like plausible instructions for behaving as intended by Anthropic (Figure 4)."  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author) 
  > "It seems hard to make the model think in a similar way without instructing the model about what it is supposed to do, but if instructions for the behavior are in the prompt, that might make various detection strategies work much better in a disanalogous way."  
  > -- `research__reducing_risk_from_scheming_by_studying_trained_in_188311dd` (2025-10-16; solo author)

9. **Prefers a priori plausible beliefs and normal-looking setups over unusual scenarios** because smarter models notice and disregard implausible information.

  > "As AIs get smarter, they will be better at noticing and disregarding implausible information, so it might be very important that the information is a priori plausible."  
  > -- `research__prospects_for_studying_actual_schemers_c74df8d5` (2025-09-19; first author) 
  > "the models do find our setup less plausible, a setup with a more normal training criteria or a more expected training criteria. So it's like, you know, there's some amount to which they can realize it's fake"  
  > -- `research__inference_scaling_alignment_faking_deal_making_fro_eeec16bb` (2025-02-20; solo author)

10. **Prefers evidence that is egregious, consistent and not salience-primed over demonstrations where the scenario makes the behaviour salient** because primed behaviour says little about natural scheming.

  > "in both demonstrating plausible consistency (e.g. not occurring at a time when subversion has been made so salient), egregiousness, and general competence."  
  > -- `research__how_will_we_update_about_scheming_f0cc5a1c` (2025-01-06; solo author) 
  > "Directly instructing the model not to fake alignment increases alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap, perhaps because it makes this behavior more salient"  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author)

11. **Prefers many ablations and matched controls over trusting a single prompt** because one prompt may leak the desired behaviour or install non-robust heuristics.

  > "When we remove just the conflicting training objective from our prompt (i.e., that the training objective is to never refuse, or to dismiss animal welfare), we see alignment-faking reasoning and the compliance gap disappear completely"  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author) 
  > "small variations in the prompt that prior to RL had no substantial effect on the compliance gap—such as swapping the AI company from “Anthropic” to “OpenAI”—now greatly increase the compliance gap"  
  > -- `research__alignment_faking_in_large_language_models_19a35a5c` (2024-12-18; first author)

12. **Prefers causal manipulation of eval awareness or in-context evidence over passive observation** because it shows the factor actually drives behaviour.

  > "Anthropic identified internal representations (SAE features and vectors from contrastive pairs) which may relate to eval awareness, then selectively inhibited these representations when evaluating models. [...] Inhibiting random representations, in contrast, didn't have substantial effects."  
  > -- `research__sonnet_4_5_s_eval_gaming_seriously_undermines_alig_28cd2450` (2025-10-30; last author) 
  > "The fact that instruction violation increases as the score for violating instructions increases shows that the score values seen by the model causally change the instruction violation rate. This method of establishing causation is sometimes called a “dose response.”"  
  > -- `research__towards_understanding_score_seeking_in_llms_12d49b8b` (2026-10-29; middle author)

13. **Prefers delivering context via environment artifacts or tool results the model must read or infer over stating it in the prompt** because this keeps beliefs in-context and less staged.

  > "Here, the models must infer the run’s context from files in the environment to figure out which grader will evaluate the run, unlike the earlier case, where they only had to read a file that stated the purpose"  
  > -- `research__towards_understanding_score_seeking_in_llms_12d49b8b` (2026-10-29; middle author) 
  > "System prompting is the weakest intervention, while a fictional agent encountering contradictory evidence on the web is the strongest."  
  > -- `research__believe_it_or_not_how_deeply_dollms_believe_implan_0dbfa6a5` (2025-10-20; middle author)

14. **Prefers behaviour-grounded evidence over internals-only or self-report evidence** because behaviour is what convinces people and self-report misses action-level misalignment.

  > "More generally, I think that to convince people enough to take strong action, evidence will need to bottom out in some sort of behavioral evidence that (many) humans can understand."  
  > -- `research__to_be_legible_evidence_of_misalignment_probably_ha_98888866` (2025-04-15; solo author) 
  > "The generalization doesn't extend to broad misalignment, and we checked this behaviorally, not just by asking the models about themselves."  
  > -- `research__reward_hacking_without_egregious_misalignment_in_a_90723a37` (2026-06-24; last author)

15. **Prefers claiming that realism is helpful but insufficient over treating it as a solution** because future models will distinguish highly realistic evals from deployment.

  > "Caveat: As noted before, we don't expect eval realism to scale indefinitely to future models, which will eventually distinguish highly realistic evals from deployment."  
  > -- `research__sonnet_4_5_s_eval_gaming_seriously_undermines_alig_28cd2450` (2025-10-30; last author) 
  > "the model might be aware it is in a test even when it doesn't mention this in its chain-of-thought. So, suppressing internal representations (even when this reduces the model's verbalized eval awareness to zero) might not succeed in making the model totally unaware it is in an evaluation."  
  > -- `research__sonnet_4_5_s_eval_gaming_seriously_undermines_alig_28cd2450` (2025-10-30; last author)

16. **Prefers keeping held-out evals free of optimisation pressure over training on them** because training on the test teaches the model to play to the test.

  > "There’s lots of ways to accidentally put optimization pressure on all sorts of properties of the AI’s behavior and cognition that were intended to be held out, leading to Goodharting, which can lead you to be radically misled by your evaluations"  
  > -- `research__anthropic_repeatedly_accidentally_trained_against__00aa44f5` (2026-04-14; last author) 
  > "A simple way to put this is that "it seems bad to train on the test if training is mostly making the model play to the test", which seems sensible enough."  
  > -- `research__sonnet_4_5_s_eval_gaming_seriously_undermines_alig_28cd2450` (2025-10-30; last author)
